lesson.title: When Averages Lie: Unmasking Simpson's Paradox
lesson.summary: Simpson's paradox occurs when a trend that appears in every subgroup of data reverses or vanishes once the subgroups are combined, usually because a lurking variable is unevenly distributed between the groups being compared.
lesson.body:
Imagine two university applicant groups, and every single program shows Group 2 being admitted at a higher rate than Group 1, yet when you pool every program together, Group 1 comes out ahead overall. That is not a typo and it is not bad arithmetic. It is Simpson's paradox, a phenomenon in which a trend that holds within every subgroup of data reverses once the subgroups are combined into one overall figure.

Simpson's paradox happens because a combined rate is not a simple average of two group rates, it is a weighted average, and the weights themselves can hide important information. Whenever the groups being compared are also associated with some third variable, a lurking variable, that affects the outcome and is distributed unevenly between the groups, combining the raw data can scramble the direction of the association you actually care about. The paradox is a warning label attached to the idea of association itself: an association visible in combined data can be an artifact of a lurking variable rather than a real relationship between the two variables you set out to study.

Consider Westfield University, which admits applicants from two pools, Group 1 and Group 2, into two programs. In the Design program, Group 1 is admitted 240 out of 320 times, which is 75%, while Group 2 is admitted 68 out of 80 times, which is 85%. In the Engineering program, Group 1 is admitted 8 out of 80 times, which is 10%, while Group 2 is admitted 48 out of 320 times, which is 15%. Group 2 has the higher admission rate in both programs individually. Now look at the totals. Group 1 overall: 248 admitted out of 400 applicants, which is 62%. Group 2 overall: 116 admitted out of 400 applicants, which is 29%. Combined across both programs, Group 1's admission rate is more than double Group 2's, even though Group 2 did better in each program separately.

The reversal is not a coincidence, it is arithmetic. Group 1 sent 320 of its 400 applicants, 80%, to the easier Design program, where admission rates are high for everyone. Group 2 sent 320 of its 400 applicants, 80%, to the harder Engineering program, where admission rates are low for everyone. Program choice, acting as a lurking variable here, is unevenly distributed between the two applicant groups and is strongly related to the outcome, so it dominates the combined figures even though Group 2 genuinely outperforms Group 1 within each program.

The practical lesson is that a combined statistic can be actively misleading, and the fix is not a different formula but a different question: is there a lurking variable that differs between the groups being compared and that also affects the outcome? Whenever a headline claims one hospital, one school, or one treatment outperforms another based on combined data, Simpson's paradox is a reason to ask how the underlying subgroups were weighted before accepting the combined comparison at face value. This same instinct, distrusting a raw comparison until you know how groups were formed and weighted, is exactly what motivates the deliberate design of experiments, which the rest of this unit builds from the ground up.
